# 劳动·工具·工艺 {.unnumbered}



> 本主题共 13 篇语境短文。每篇把一批旧词织进一个场景；目标词**加粗**，展开"本篇生词"可遮释义自测。



### The Workshop at Dawn

Before the sun clears the ridge, the old joiner is already at his bench. Beside him sits a **bunk** of rough timber — planks stripped straight off the trunk he helped **log** last autumn. He picks up a chisel and works the face of the wood until it is **hewn** smooth, then reaches into his **kit** for the finishing tools: a worn **iron**, a jar of **wax**, and a fistful of **cord** to bind the joints tight. A **hook** screwed into the wall holds his **hose** for wetting the sharpening stone. The **coal** stove in the corner has been burning since before he woke; the **coke** it leaves behind will be shoveled into a **bin** near the door come evening.

His wife works at the table across the room, threading a needle to **sew** a tear in the canvas apron. She pulls **lint** from the **batt** inside a quilted pad, pressing the cotton flat with her palm, then uses a length of **cord** already cut to edge the hem. A tin **mug** of cold tea sits at her elbow, its handle hooked on a **nail** driven into a post years ago. She keeps her thread and **nib** pens and ink in the same **kit** box, orderly as always.

Outside, the younger hand fills a **pail** from the rain barrel and carries it to the vegetable bed they mean to **pave** along the edge with flat stone. He will **mow** the long grass near the fence once the dew lifts, then join the others hauling the season's **load** down to the **mine** entrance before noon. A scrap of **pell** tacked to the barn door lists the day's tasks in blunt letters. The **gear** is ready: ropes **coil**ed on the cart, a **net** folded over the side rail, the old **plow** oiled and waiting. What needs **darn**ing will be darned tonight, and what needs **wax** will be waxed — there is no rushing the craft, only doing it right.

### 棚屋里的一个工作日

The old **shed** behind the mill had seen generations of labour. Each morning, the foreman would step inside, hang his coat on the **rack**, and begin. The day's first task was paper: raw **pulp** hauled in on flat **slab**s of compressed fibre, ready to be pressed and dried. While the press ran, he used a **pump** to clear standing water from the floor — the drainage here was never quite right.

Outside, two workers moved across the yard. One dragged a **rake** across the gravel path, collecting wood shavings into neat windrows before they could **seam** into the wet ground. The other swung a **broom**, its **besom** head worn almost flat, then switched to a **brush** to work the grime out of the **bench** joints. A copper **tray** nearby held small parts sorted by size: **tack**s, **stud**s, and a folded strip of **tain** that someone had peeled from an old mould.

By mid-morning the heavier work began. The **crane** swung a **crate** of raw ore over the furnace pit; the melt would leave a thick skin of **slag** once it cooled. A **cable** steadied the load while a younger apprentice applied the **brake** just before the crate touched down. At the casting bench, sheets of finished metal were cut — one destined to become **tyre** stock, another to be punched into **tile** blanks. A **clamp** held each sheet fast while the cutter scored it. Scrap ends went down the **chute** into a bin below.

The afternoon belonged to finishing. One craftsman stirred a **churn** of sizing compound, ladling it over coarse cloth. Another fitted the last panel of the **coupe** body, seating each **stud** with a single clean stroke. The walls of the room were lined with **couch**es of cured leather — raw stock waiting for the saddler. A small **caddy** on the shelf held spare blades, a cake of **soap** for lubricating the saw, and a curl of spare **cable**. By dusk the crew had loaded the finished pieces onto a flatbed, ready for the **rake** of morning light and whatever the next order required — though tonight they would **reap** the quiet satisfaction of a clean, emptied shop.

### The Craftsman's Workshop at the End of the Day

The old workshop smelled of **rosin** and hot **steel**. Along the back wall, a **lathe** hummed steadily as the apprentice turned a cabinet leg to a perfect taper, its **shaft** gleaming under the lamp. Nearby, the senior smith had begun to **forge** a set of door brackets over the coal hearth, his hammer ringing against iron while sparks fell like brief stars onto the **scrap** pile at his feet. A **mason** worked at the far bench, fitting **tiles** with a small rubber mallet, pausing now and then to run a thumb along each edge and check the **hinge** alignment on the panel he was building into the wall.

On the central worktable sat the smaller tools of the trade: a **drill** resting beside a jar of cutting oil, a coil of **latex** tubing used to protect finished edges during clamping, a tin of **satin** varnish half-stirred, and a **flask** of mineral spirits for cleaning brushes. A **sieve** hung from a nail overhead, used each morning to strain old finish before it went back into the can. Beside it dangled a **sling** rigged for lifting the heavy kilns shelf, and a wooden-handled **razor** kept solely for scoring veneer. The **stave** of a barrel being repaired leaned in the corner, its grain still dark with old wine.

Outside, the yard held its own quiet industry. The groundskeeper ran a pair of **rakes** across the gravel, pausing to pry up a **divot** of grass that had crept in from the lawn. The kiln tender checked the **kilns** temperature with a long iron rod, then used a **ladle** to pour a test pour of glaze into a mold. A boy stamped receipts with the workshop's **dater**, filed the **stubs** into a binder, and carried the day's offcuts — odd **prong**s, bent **screws**, a snapped **karts** axle from a repair job, a warped **grate** from the forge room — to the scrap bin. Someone had left a half-finished **quilt** block on the window ledge, its patches arranged but not yet stitched, a quiet contrast to all the metal and stone. The shop cat, indifferent to the **grind** of the angle grinder starting up again inside, stretched out across a bolt of **satin** left for re-upholstery and went back to sleep.

### The Craftsman's Workshop at First Light

Before the **diesel** engine outside had time to warm up, the old craftsman was already at his bench. He pulled a worn **towel** from the hook by the **faucet**, ran it under cold water, and wrung it out — a small ritual before the serious work began. The **drawer** beside him held his most trusted instruments: a **chisel** whose handle had been worn smooth by decades of use, a set of **gauges** for reading metal thickness, and a small **gimbal** mount he'd salvaged from a broken **glider** rigging years ago. Each tool had its place, and each place had its purpose.

The morning's main job was annealing a set of steel **blades**. To **anneal** them properly, he'd heat each one to a deep orange glow, then let it cool slowly in the **bucket** of fine sand on the floor. Beside it sat a rack of parts already **forged** the previous day — rough, heavy things waiting to be refined. He used a **wedge** to separate two pieces that had stuck together in the cooling tray, tapping it in with a mallet until he felt the seam give. A metal **funnel** directed quench oil into a small trough without splashing, and a **damper** on the furnace door let him control the airflow without opening it all the way.

By mid-morning he had shifted to lighter tasks. He spread a length of woven **fabric** across the worktable to protect the surface, then set out a row of **enamel**-coated hardware he needed to inspect for cracks. A **buzzer** on the wall sounded when the kiln reached temperature — he'd wired it himself from spare parts, a modest **gadget** that saved him constant checking. The **fender** panels leaning against the far wall were next: he would **bleach** the rust stains first, then prime and coat. Old **tyres** were stacked outside near the **corral** fence, earmarked for a neighbour who patched them for resale. A roll of **vinyl** sheeting lay beside them, useful for waterproofing the storage shed once he got around to it.

Lunch came and went. In the afternoon he turned to the kitchen fittings his daughter had brought over — a dripping **faucet** valve, a rusted **grater**, a chipped carton of tile adhesive. He opened the **carton** of **cement** compound, gave it a **whisk** with a mixing rod until the lumps dissolved, then packed the cracked grout line with a small trowel. The garden bed outside had a long **furrow** he'd dug the week before for drainage pipe; he used a spare **bucket** to carry the excess cement out rather than let it harden on the floor. A **butler**'s pantry shelf — a refinishing job he'd promised a neighbour — was propped in the corner, its surface masked off with tape, waiting for the final coat.

At dusk he checked the **vinyl** membrane on the shed roof, tightened the bolts on the **fender** brackets, and ran a damp **towel** over the **blades** to wipe off the oil film. The **diesel** generator ticked as it cooled. He switched off the light, shut the **damper** on the stove, and left everything as he had found it — orderly, purposeful, ready for tomorrow.

### The Yard at First Light

Before the **hooter** had finished its long cry, the crew was already moving. The **roster** pinned to the shed door listed twenty names — **hauler**s, cutters, and smiths — each assigned a post before sunrise. At the **quarry** face, workers pried loose great slabs that the **ripper** tore into workable sections; **rubble** and **sliver**s of stone rattled down the slope and were carted away. A veteran mason crouched by the wheel of a cart, peeling back the cracked **hubcap** and packing **grease** into the axle housing before the load runs began.

Inside the workshop, the air smelled of cut **lumber** and hot metal. An apprentice reached for the **pliers**, then thought better of it and grabbed the **mallet** instead, coaxing a copper fitting into its **socket** without leaving a dent. Beside him, an older smith kept **hammer**ing a blank on the anvil — steady, unhurried — pausing only to test the edge with his thumb before sliding the blade back onto the **honing** stone. The **jigsaw** whined in the corner where a joiner was cutting curves for a new gate; when he finished, he set the panels between **levers** to hold them square while the glue cured.

Out in the yard the **herder** — who also kept the tool register — walked the fence line, checking every **paling** for rot. The **shears** had already been through the wool shed; fleece still lay piled against the wall, waiting to be **sifted** for debris. The soil plot beyond the fence had been turned and freshly **manure**d, dark and steaming in the cool air. A **nozzle** hose ran along the furrows. Someone had left a **saddle** draped over the gate post — the **hauler** who brought in the timber delivery had tethered his horse there at dawn.

By midday the foreman called a halt so the metallurgist could **refine** the alloy batch and **recast** the flawed bracket that had failed inspection the week before. The **nickel** content had been wrong. He did not **resign** himself to the loss; instead he pulled out his notes, chose to **render** the whole pour again, and asked the crew to **resume** their stations once the mold was set. No one objected. Work like this — patient, precise, repeated — was simply what the yard asked of everyone who stayed.

### The Forge, the Floor, and the Finer Work

At dawn, the **foundry** roared to life. The head **welder** tightened his **harness**, set his **headset** over his ears to block the noise, and bent over the glowing joint. His apprentice steadied the workpiece against a battered **tripod** while molten slag dripped onto the stone floor. Nearby, a **grinder** screamed against raw iron, throwing a fan of orange sparks across the wall — walls still rough with old **stucco** that someone had plastered on decades ago and never sanded smooth. Above the **furnace**, a ventilation **string** of ducts ran to the roof, each section **splice**d together with riveted flanges the old-timers had taught them to make by hand. On the rack hung iron rods and **staves** cut to length, waiting to be shaped.

The **tinker** who kept the small tools in order shuffled in with a **dustpan** of metal filings and a **trowel** he had borrowed from the masonry crew next door. He worked through his **checkin** list methodically — noting which drill **spikes** had gone dull, which **wrench** had a cracked handle, which **leather** grip needed replacing. His long **tenure** in the shop had taught him that a careless **stitch** on a glove or a poorly spliced cable could send a man to the infirmary before lunch. He moved like a man who understood **techne** not as a word but as a practice: the quiet knowledge living in the hands.

By midmorning a **tailor** from the uniform depot arrived carrying a **vessel** of rivets and a bolt of canvas. He spread his work across the **armrest** of a salvage chair, measuring and cutting without a template — he had long since memorized every standard cut. On the far side of the building the night-shift crew had **stoped** a new gallery in the coal seam; a **stoper** still stood propped against the wall, its piston caked with grey dust. A **bellhop** from the site office jogged across the yard to deliver a revised drawing, and the foreman paused just long enough to **archive** the old one in the flat-file cabinet before pinning the new one up. Outside, a stack of **coalite** briquettes sat under a tarpaulin — the winter fuel reserve. The morning's work was ordinary in every detail, and irreplaceable in every hand that did it.

### The Sawmill at the Edge of Town

The old **sawmill** had been running since before anyone could remember. **Sawdust** coated every surface — the rafters, the windowsills, the **shutters** that clapped open each morning at first light. At the centre of the floor, a great **spindle** drove the main blade, its rotation powered by a small **turbine** fed by the millrace out back. When the belt slipped, the foreman would reach into his **toolkit**, pull out a **spanner**, and set things right before the next log arrived on the chain.

Outside, the season's work spread across the yard. A **tractor** dragged freshly felled timber from the tree line while a crew was already **plowing** the mud flat to lay a new foundation for the drying shed. Nearby, the **plumber** crouched over a burst pipe, working a **plunger** against the blockage with steady, practiced force. A **thimble** of solder sat warming on a brick beside him. Further along, two apprentices were **spliced** into the rigging of a scaffold — one **sifting** lime powder through a fine screen, the other **mudding** the interior wall with long, even strokes of the float.

The yard **steward** — a gruff woman who had **oversaw** every major project here for twenty years, just as she had **oversee** the new hires today — moved between stations with a clipboard and a thermos of black coffee under her arm. She had once driven a **minivan** full of visiting inspectors around a site like this and answered every question without checking a note. Now a **proctor** from the regional guild stood at her shoulder, watching the **reaping** crew collect bundled rye from the far field, observing the orchard gang finish their **pruning**, and ticking items off a form on his **monitor**. The guild cared about process: every **shutoff** valve labelled, every **nibbler** and die accounted for in the stores, even the small **widgets** that coupled the air lines.

In the forge at the back, the **smelter** glowed orange. A smith drew out a **wrought** iron bracket, cooling it just enough before setting it on the anvil. The **shutter** above the hearth was propped open with a stick. On the wall hung a faded blueprint, its corners held by four magnets — the kind of drawing made when craft still lived in the hands of people who knew that good work, whether **reaping** grain or casting metal, was never an accident.

### The Workshop at Dusk

The old boatyard sat on cemented ground beside the river, where a **flatboat** had been hauled up for its seasonal **overhaul**. A mechanic checked the **odometer** on the yard's utility cart, then pulled the **dipstick** to confirm the oil level before the next shift. Nearby, a welder was cutting steel with a loud **chainsaw**-like grinder, the **grinding** shriek bouncing off corrugated walls. Paint cans rested inside a metal **canister** rack, and an **atomizer** sat on the shelf above, used to apply a fine protective mist on finished surfaces. Against the far wall, a worn **mattress** stuffed into an **armchair** served as the unofficial break spot—**in-house** comfort at its most honest.

In the mixing room, a cook-turned-craftsman lifted a heavy **cauldron** off the burner and poured the molten sealant through a **colander** to filter out debris. A **cleanser** spray and several rags hung by the door. The walls showed **layering** upon **layering** of old paint—**concrete** evidence of decades of work. A junior technician was **laminate**-pressing wood panels for a cabinet order, while the foreman sorted **clerical** paperwork that tracked every job: **cropping** records, materials logs, delivery schedules. Their combined **endeavor** kept the yard solvent through slow seasons.

Outside, the yard's retired founder—now an **emeritus** director—stood watching a small **aviation** enthusiast assemble a model aircraft, carefully shaping the **fuselage** with a hobby knife. The boy had arrived with a **backpack** full of tools and enough **manpower**—all his own—to finish by nightfall. The **plumbing** under the workshop eaves dripped steadily, and through a **peephole** in the fence a neighbor tracked the **dredging** barge at work mid-river, its **logistic** precision impressive against the slow current.

### The Yard, the Workshop, the Long Day

Early morning, before the foreman arrived, the crew dragged a **portable** generator across the gravel and positioned it beside the half-built wall. The old **radiator** had been patched and rehung, part of a **revamped** heating circuit that nobody fully trusted yet. Above them, planks of **scaffold** stretched three storeys high, the steel pipes cold and slick with dew. One of the younger men took a **scrubber** to the stained concrete blocks, the **scouring** loud enough to drown out conversation. A **shredder** hummed near the skip, chewing through the **cardboard** packaging that had piled up overnight.

By midmorning the **bulldozer** had **compacted** the fill layer flat, and the **compactor** made a second pass to be sure. A mason worked at the base of the wall, **cementing** each course with the quiet patience his trade demanded — this was clearly a **vocation**, not just a job. Nearby, the **artisanal** tile-setter laid each piece by hand, a deliberate contrast to the machines idling behind him. His **apparatus** was simple: a notched trowel, a rubber mallet, a bucket. The kitchen **utensils** for the site canteen had been **assembled** in a crate on the **tailgate** of the supply truck; the **chauffeur**-driver climbed down and unlatched it without ceremony.

Afternoon light caught the blades of a small **windmill** mounted on the fence — someone's idea of a wind gauge. The site supervisor **shepherded** the apprentices from station to station, pausing to demonstrate how to use the **wrenches** without stripping a bolt. One apprentice tried to **shoehorn** an oversized pipe fitting into a bracket three sizes too small; the supervisor stopped him with a look. The **throttle** on the concrete mixer was sticky, worn from months of **slogging** through long pours. A **camcorder** on a tripod recorded the progress for the client report. By dusk, the site's **concierge**-equivalent — the gateman who logged every delivery — was tallying the day's **spoilage** against the materials sheet, the numbers not as bad as feared. The crew began to **construct** what they hoped would be the final section before the weekend. Every **appliance**, every hand tool, every body on that scaffold had earned its place.

### The Workshop and Its Keepers

The old workshop had stood for three generations. Its current **custodian**, a retired machinist named Harald, arrived each morning with a **broomstick** in one hand and a clipboard in the other, determined first to **declutter** the benches before any real work began. He would wipe down the surfaces with **detergent**, stack the raw **porcelain** blanks in the drying rack, and pin the day's job orders to the board with a **thumbtack**.

Harald's young **apprentice**, Selin, had come to him not from a school of fine arts but straight after finishing her **doctorate** in materials science — an unusual path that raised eyebrows until people saw her work. She knew how to read a **rectifier** panel, could explain why **tempering** made a blade less brittle, and understood instinctively that copper was **malleable** enough to be pressed into the intricate grooves of a mold without cracking. Her first assignment was to **refurbish** a seized **alternator** salvaged from a decommissioned boat. She had to **dismantle** it bolt by bolt, **replenish** the lubricant reservoir, and test the **interlock** before reassembly. Beside her on the bench sat a set of **binoculars** she used to inspect the hairline tolerances on the shaft — a habit she'd picked up at sea.

The workshop also built small watercraft. On the far wall hung an **outrigger** frame waiting to be fitted. Nearby, a half-finished hull was wrapped in **cellophane** to keep sawdust off the gelcoat. The **propeller** for the hull lay clamped in a vice while Selin filed its edges, pausing now and then to consult a sketch inked on a scrap of **parchment** she kept rolled under the **sideboard**. The **lawnmower** engine donated by a neighbor was being repurposed as a test rig — an odd sight, but it let them spin the shaft under load without risking the real motor. A **sprinkler** head salvaged from a demolished factory ceiling had been rigged above the grinder as a makeshift coolant nozzle, a small improvisation that showed how craftspeople **synergize** whatever is at hand.

Harald's role had never quite fit a single title. The letterhead of the cooperative listed him as **secretary**, yet his actual work was to **supervise** every project from intake to delivery, to **undertake** the negotiations with suppliers, and — when a journeyman was let go for shoddy finishing — to draft the **dismissal** notice himself, a task he hated. He never **fabricate**d reasons; he stated facts plainly and moved on. That directness was part of what kept the workshop's reputation intact across decades, outlasting fashions the way good **porcelain** outlasts the table it sits on.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

### The Workshop, the Field, and the Town Beyond

The old **husbandman** rose before dawn. His **occupation** was simple enough to name but endless in its demands: tend the soil, keep the tools, bring in what the season offered. By the time light reached the barn, he had already walked the rows where **cultivation** had softened the earth into dark ribbons, and the first crew was out **harvesting** the last of the summer grain with practiced strokes.

Inside the main shed, a younger craftsman was at the forge. He worked in **fabricated** steel, shaping parts for a small press—a **contraption** of levers and gears that the cooperative had designed to replace three hours of hand labor. The machine's **crankshaft** lay on the bench beside a bicycle **derailleur** someone had brought in for repair, its teeth worn thin from a season of hill roads. The **windshield** of the workshop's delivery truck leaned against the far wall, cracked and waiting to be replaced; the replacement pane sat in a **ventilated** storage cabinet so the adhesive would cure properly. Nearby, a rack held sets of **auxiliaries**—clamps, dies, and guides—alongside a roll of **waterproof** canvas for wrapping finished parts during transport.

Down the lane stood the guild hall, which served as both **repository** and classroom. Its shelves held a dense **compilation** of trade manuals, pattern books, and old **boilerplate** contracts going back two generations. A weaver displayed her **handicraft** on the long table: a **breastplate**-shaped ceremonial piece woven in silver thread, its **upholstery**-style backing padded and stitched by hand. Beside it sat a tray of **earthenware** cups fired that week, and a cabinet of polished **silverware** awaiting an estate order. One corner was given over to a small still; the guild had been running a **distilling** operation for medicinal spirits since the previous century, and the copper fittings were checked monthly.

Outside, a crew was **excavating** the foundation for a new storage annex, working carefully around the water line. The site foreman kept a **bulletproof** case of survey instruments locked in his truck. Back in the village proper, the **laundromat** hummed beside the hardware supply; its large windows were steamed, and a hand-lettered sign listed **janitorial** supplies for sale inside. The **undertaker**'s shop stood quietly at the corner, its window dressed with **deliverable** urns and memorial pieces waiting for collection. A cargo van idled in front, its side panels marked with the cooperative's logo, loading the last **discharging** run of the day—boxes broken down and stacked flat after a morning of **dismantling** a decommissioned textile frame. The town's shared **facilities** kept everything moving: the loading dock, the cold store, the repair bay—each one worn smooth by years of use and still entirely adequate.

### The Workshop, the Site, and the Office Behind Them

Dawn had barely broken when the first shift arrived at the **fabrication** shed. Under close **supervision**, a veteran **woodworking** craftsman guided two apprentices through the morning's tasks: one pair worked on a cedar screen, threading thin rods through a **latticework** of oak strips, while the other assembled a small gate, driving each bolt tight with a **screwdriver**. A bucket of **lubrication** sat nearby for the hinge sets. Beside the bench, a worn **wheelbarrow** waited to ferry off-cuts to the yard. Down the corridor a **glassblower** — one of only three **commissioned** artisans on the floor — shaped molten glass into lamp covers, each finished globe showing a neat **perforation** ring at the base where the cord would pass. The walls themselves were an older kind of craft: **Wattle and Dab**, the mud-and-wicker technique that had kept buildings standing for centuries before **manufactured** board ever existed.

Outside, the canal-extension crew was already deep in the muck. The project had begun as a modest **canalization** scheme, but a late **consultation** with the regional authority had widened the scope considerably. The site foreman — a quiet **practitioner** of old-school earthworks — had submitted a formal **requisition** for two extra **sledgehammer** sets and a concrete vibrator. **Implementation** of the revised plan fell to him the moment the contractor chose to **take charge** without calling a proper handover meeting, an act that triggered the previous supervisor's quiet **resignation**. Nobody blamed him; the project's **stewardship** had been muddled for months.

By mid-afternoon the **headquarter** of the civil works firm — a glass tower three kilometres away — hummed with a different kind of labour. A **receptionist** at the front desk logged visitor passes while procurement reviewed the **requisition** slips from the site. Several engineers were in **telecommuting** mode, joining the budget call from home; one had only just managed to **get off work** in time to collect his car from **valet parking** before the garage closed. A **white-collar** project manager drafted the **undertaking** letter that would bind both parties to the new timeline, her language careful and formal. Nearby, a younger colleague — fresh out of an **apprenticeship** programme — updated a **do-it-yourself** punch-list template he had built himself, proof that a little initiative goes a long way when no one hands you the tools.

### The Last Details Before the Road

At the edge of the garage, a single **lighting fixture** cast a warm cone of light over the hood of the old truck. The mechanic reached across the wiper arm and clicked the replacement **windshield wiper** into place with a satisfying snap — the kind of small, clean motion that signals a job done right.
